summary: A concrete lighthouse of 1934 on Navy Hill above Garapan, Saipan, built under Japanese rule; damaged in 1944, a restaurant in the 1990s, and awarded for a visitor center in 2026.

structures.note: Three-story concrete tower. DeWire gives about 43 ft (13.1 m); the 1974 nomination gives no height. The concrete is ash from burned coral and seashells with crushed coral aggregate, a poor grade that weathers easily (nomination).

Keepers' dwelling abutting the tower. The nomination describes three first-floor rooms around a circular porch; DeWire, citing Lotz, describes a two-story dwelling with five first-floor rooms. Its lower story was partly leveled after the war (DeWire).
Concrete foundation of an auxiliary generator about fifty feet north of the tower (nomination).

access.note: No public opening hours in the sources. The property was awarded to the Marianas Visitors Authority in 2026 and site clearing began in July 2026. Do not enter the tower while work continues.

facts.agency: Department of Public Lands, Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (property, awarded 2026 to the Marianas Visitors Authority); the 1974 nomination names the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands as owner

events.note: Built by the Japanese administration to guide ships into Tanapag Harbor; one of twelve navigation lights Japan erected on and around Saipan.
June 1944: Japanese forces put out the Garapan light to prevent it from aiding the American landing; Japanese soldiers used the tower as a lookout.
American bombardment and the battle damaged the concrete walls and the lighting apparatus.

Nomination: the light ceased to function in 1944 because of the American bombardment and was never rebuilt or used again. DeWire says a small light ran until at least July 1947. The sources conflict; see notes.
Seabees of the 177th Battalion repaired the tower toward the end of the war for use as an observation and communications post (year approximate).
Light in use at least until 18 July 1947, when the Navy left Saipan (DeWire).
Nominated by David T. Lotz, Marianas parks planner, 29 November 1974; listed on the National Register in December 1974.

Early 1990s (year approximate): a business owner expressed interest in the lighthouse; it was later refitted as a restaurant, with an open-air terrace on the second level and a fiberglass roof on top. DeWire gives no date for the refit.
The restaurant closed about five years after it opened (year approximate, from DeWire).
Saipan Lighthouse Historical Society established; volunteers cleaned the site and painted the tower.
Plans to restore the lighthouse and convert it into a visitor center for the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument. Funding had not materialized by 2016.
Typhoon Soudelor tore the fiberglass roof off the lighthouse; the tower and lower section withstood the winds.
Property recently awarded by the Department of Public Lands to the Marianas Visitors Authority for its headquarters (article of 1 July 2026).
July 2026: site clearing began. The authority plans a visitor and cultural experience center, dependent on funding; it expects to move in before December 2026.

notes_for_editor: 1. Wartime and postwar use conflict: the 1974 nomination says the light was never rebuilt or used again after the 1944 damage; DeWire (2016, citing a Seabee repair, a 1946 Hydrographic Office report and the Navy's departure on 18 July 1947) says a small light ran until at least 1947. The record's deactivated year (1944) follows the nomination. The story gives both. A 1945-1947 light list or Navy record would settle it; none was found. 2. Height: DeWire 43 ft; Wikipedia gives about 50 ft (not cited). The story uses 43 ft with attribution. 3. Dwelling: the nomination describes three rooms around a circular porch on the first floor; DeWire, citing Lotz, says a two-story dwelling with five first-floor rooms. Not stated in the story. 4. Lamp: the 1946 Hydrographic Office characteristic (flash 1 s, eclipse 5 s) is DeWire's citation of that report; the report itself was not read, so no light characteristic is entered in facts. 5. Journal title: the PDF's running heads read 'International Lighthouse, Spring 2016' on some pages and 'The Keeper's Log, Spring 2016' on others. Confirm before publishing the citation. 6. Typhoon: DeWire's text says the typhoon tore the fiberglass roof off; a photo caption says it tore off the cupola and damaged the structure. The story uses the text. 7. Harbor: the nomination says the light was built to guide ships into Tanapag Harbor; DeWire says it overlooks Garapan Harbor. Both are in the story. 8. The 1934 date is in the nomination and DeWire. DeWire's line that the light had been 'shining for a decade when World War II began' does not fit a 1934 build and is not used. 9. Keepers: no keeper is named in the nomination, DeWire or the 2026 article. The keepers chapter is omitted. Japanese colonial-era records were not searched; they are not in the local corpus. 10. Marianas Variety (2021, 'Mariana Lighthouse reopens') could not be fetched (HTTP 429 on two tries). The 2021 renovation and reopening as a restaurant appear in Wikipedia and a social-media post only, so the story does not state them. Recheck the Marianas Variety article when the rate limit clears. 11. Position: the record's point (15.211765, 145.731663) matches Wikipedia's coordinates; the nomination gives only corner coordinates. No correction. 12. Access and safety: no current opening hours found; the site is under clearing for the Marianas Visitors Authority (July 2026); DeWire's 2015 visitor was warned against going alone. 13. Storms: Typhoon Soudelor (2015) is the only storm in the sources read. The 2026 article mentions recovery from Super Typhoon Sinlaku; not used. 14. No newspaper search was run for this station (budget). Japanese-language sources were not read.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination says the light ceased in 1944; DeWire has it in use until 1947. The story presents the nomination's statement and DeWire's account side by side and does not choose between them.
